description: We’re a team of curious, driven students who love turning ideas into working solutions. Our interests range from full-stack development, AI/ML and embedded systems to creative problem-solving that demands critical thinking. We believe the best solutions come from collaboration, combining our different perspectives to push every build further. At this hackathon, we aim to tackle real-world problems, learn something new and, most importantly, have a whole lot of fun!
summary: AstroNova is a free browser game where players design, launch and fly a complete space mission. A fading radio signal from Ceruvia, a fictional icy moon, sets up five missions, from a small Earth-observing satellite to a sample return and the trip to Ceruvia. In each mission, players pick a science goal first, build a spacecraft from 32 parts while trading off mass, fuel, power, data, budget and time, choose a rocket, route, orbit and ground stations, pass a launch review split into NASA's launch, space, ground and user segments, fly each phase in short arcade minigames, and report on the science they found. Every engineering decision has a visible consequence and there is no single right answer, which turns abstract mission trade-offs into choices students can feel and learn from. It runs on any phone or computer with no install, has a very forgiving Beginner mode, and supports online co-op for 2 to 4 players.
details:
What it does

AstroNova is a space mission design game with a five-mission campaign: an Earth-observing satellite (Shakedown), a Moon lander on the far side (Quiet Side), an asteroid sample return (Pebble Run), a Mars mission with a dust storm (Red Shadow), and finally a mission to the icy moon Ceruvia with a deadline and a trip home (Last Signal). Each mission follows the same five phases, shown on a phase bar labelled with JPL's Concept Maturity Levels: Science goal, Design, Review, Fly, Report.

How it works

Science goal: players choose a prime goal. Each goal shows who uses the data and which instruments it needs.

Design: in the hangar, players fit parts onto a spacecraft (engines, solar wings, RTGs, batteries, antennas, computers and instruments) and plan the rocket, route, orbit and ground stations. Six live meters show mass, fuel, power, budget, data and time. A Compare tab lets them run a trade study of up to three designs.

Review: a launch review checks the design and groups every item into the launch, space, ground and user segments, with a concept-of-operations timeline and a trajectory diagram for the chosen route.

Fly: players fly arcade minigames for the launch (a gravity turn), a debris field, orbit insertion, landing, a touch-and-go sample grab and reentry. The design changes how each one plays.

Science and report: players choose where to point their instruments, may land or grab samples, survive a power emergency on later missions, and get a report that scores science, objectives, piloting, data returned and budget left, with hints for anything missed and real missions similar to their design.

The engineering model is simplified, but the relationships are real: the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for fuel, sunlight falling off with the square of distance, RTG power decaying over time, battery needs in an orbit's shadow, data rates that depend on antenna, distance and ground-station time, and cost and build-and-test time.

Benefits and intended impact

Students learn mission design by making decisions and seeing the results, not by memorising formulas. There are five difficulty levels: Beginner has a coach, a "Build it for me" button and autopilots, so it is very hard to fail, while Flight Director is a real challenge. It runs on phones, tablets and computers with keyboard or touch, honours reduced-motion settings, and uses plain language throughout. Online co-op for 2 to 4 players gives each player a crew role (Mission Lead, Propulsion, Science, Power and Comms) with a GO / NO GO launch vote. Our goal is a free, open tool that teachers and students anywhere can use to understand how real science missions are planned, and why every choice is a trade-off.

Tools and technologies

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no build step. Visuals are drawn with Canvas and SVG, and sound is synthesized with the Web Audio API. Online co-op uses Firebase Authentication (anonymous) and the Realtime Database. The game is hosted on GitHub Pages and is open source under the Apache-2.0 licence. Source code: https://github.com/saket-vanga/astronova
